paragraphs.heading: Light on a surface
paragraphs.text: Luster, also spelled lustre, describes how light interacts with the surface of a mineral, a crystal or a rock. The word goes back to the Latin lux, meaning light, and it generally implies radiance, gloss or brilliance. A range of terms describe it, such as earthy, metallic, greasy and silky. Vitreous, which comes from vitrum, the Latin for glass, means a glassy luster.

paragraphs.heading: No sharp lines
paragraphs.text: Luster varies across a wide continuum, so its types have no rigid boundaries between them. That is why one mineral can often be described differently by different sources. Luster can also vary widely within one mineral species, which adds to the ambiguity. The terms are frequently combined to name in-between types, for example a "vitreous greasy" luster.

paragraphs.heading: The diamond end
paragraphs.text: Adamantine minerals have a superlative luster, seen most notably in diamond. They are transparent or translucent, and their refractive index is high, at 1.9 or more. True adamantine luster is uncommon; cerussite, zircon and cubic zirconia are examples. A lesser, but still relatively high, degree of luster is called subadamantine, as in garnet and corundum.

paragraphs.heading: Metallic and dull
paragraphs.text: Metallic minerals have the luster of polished metal, and with ideal surfaces they will work as a reflective surface. Galena, pyrite and magnetite are examples. Submetallic minerals have a luster similar to metal but are duller and less reflective. Dull, or earthy, minerals show little to no luster, because their coarse granulations scatter light in every direction.

paragraphs.heading: Glass, pearl and silk
paragraphs.text: Vitreous luster, the luster of glass, is one of the most commonly seen. It appears in minerals that are transparent or translucent and have relatively low refractive indices, such as calcite, quartz, topaz and fluorite. Pearly minerals are made of thin transparent sheets lying in the same plane, and light reflecting from these layers gives a luster that recalls pearls. Silky minerals have extremely fine fibres arranged in parallel, which gives a luster that recalls silk. Asbestos and ulexite are examples of silky minerals.

paragraphs.heading: Grease, wax and resin
paragraphs.text: Greasy minerals resemble fat or grease, and many of them also feel greasy to the touch. This luster often occurs in minerals that contain a great many microscopic inclusions, such as opal and cordierite. Waxy minerals have a luster like wax, as jade and chalcedony do. Resinous minerals look like resin, chewing gum or smooth-surfaced plastic.

paragraphs.heading: Stars and moving bands
paragraphs.text: Some minerals show unusual optical phenomena. Asterism is a luminous area in the shape of a star; it is seen in some sapphires and rubies, where impurities of rutile cause it. Chatoyant minerals show luminous bands that seem to move as the specimen is turned. Such minerals are made of parallel fibres, or contain fibrous voids or inclusions, and these reflect light so that it forms narrow bands. Tiger's eye is one of the most famous examples.
